pr_title: Respect Active Record's primary_key_type in Active Storage migrations
pr_body:
This is the simplest implementation I can think of. It checks which type is configured and uses it, or fallbacks to default.
Possibly, another, a more involved solution, is to create a new generator.

Not sure if it is worth it to extract duplicated `primary_key_type` method somewhere.

Closes #40986
cc @zzak
pr_comments: @fatkodima Can you also add a CHANGELOG and some docs? :bow:
Changed fallback, added a note to CHANGELOG and a comment to migration.
@fatkodima Could you rebase please? I will try to see if @pixeltrix can review this one 🙏
Rebased. I added an entry a little below the head of changelog to avoid further possible conflicts.
I'm wary of the changes to the historical migrations - is there a way to do this using new migrations that override the existing migration?

The migration file under `db/migrate` is only copied once when the user runs `bin/rails active_storage:install` to install Active Storage. Each migration file under `db/update_migrate` is also copied once when running the upgrade command for Active Storage, if not copied already. So, this PR does not change existing migrations in rails projects. Previously copied migrations would work as they worked when they copied back then. And when the user installs Active Storage after this PR merged, the new migration files would respect the changes in this PR.

There was a change in the main migration file recently, for example - https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/42276/files

I'm wondering whether it'd be better to generate the migration in a [similar manner to Devise][1] - that way we pick up the configuration for free. Any thoughts on this @carlosantoniodasilva? Has generating the migration caused any issues for Devise?

[1]: https://github.com/heartcombo/devise/blob/master/lib/generators/active_record/templates/migration.rb
I think that is a good idea @pixeltrix. I don't think changing that migration template on devise ever caused any problem for users.
I agree with Andrew here. I think if we want to respect the primary key type in the generators config it would be better to generate the migrations in the app instead of copying.
I'll merge this though since we can always iterate over it and this already fix one problem.

issue_context.title: active storage generator/migrations don't respect active_record's primary_key_type
issue_context.body:
Steps to repro:

Configure your app to generate tables with UUID primary keys:
config/application.rb:
```
  config.generators do |g|
    g.orm :active_record, primary_key_type: :uuid
  end
```

Run the ActiveStorage generator:
`bin/rails active_storage:install`

The generated migrations all lack the `id: :uuid` option for create_table and `type: :uuid` for foreign keys.
The `t.references :record,   null: false, polymorphic: true, index: false` is particularly concerning because it points back to normal models that (given the above application-wide configuration) likely have UUID primary keys.

Expectations:
Rails generators would honor rails configuration.  So, at a minimum all the new tables and internal relationships should use UUIDs in this case.

The `record` relationship is tricky since who knows what combination of integer/uuid/string foreign key type it should be given the app state.  That said, if the above `application.rb` config is in place, if feels like an integer is not correct.  Maybe throw a comment (or a raise statement) in that migration which calls attention to the choice the application developer needs to make?
comments:
> Run the ActiveStorage generator:
`bin/rails active_storage:install`

This command does not run a "generator" per se, but just simply copies the predefined engine's (`active_storage`) migration files (https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/activestorage/db/migrate/20170806125915_create_active_storage_tables.rb) into `db/migrations` folder.

Yes, while this feature probably will be useful, it will greatly complicate the existing code. You can always manually edit the copied migration files however you like.

@rafaelfranca Wdyt on this?

We just came across this issue. Please please, respect the PK type configured in rails. 

The logic doesn't have to be super complicated, it could be two different copies of the migration - one for uuids and one for ints.
And/or as suggested, throw an error, or print a big warning.

This issue has been automatically marked as stale because it has not been commented on for at least three months.
The resources of the Rails team are limited, and so we are asking for your help.
If you can still reproduce this error on the `6-1-stable` branch or on `main`, please reply with all of the information you have about it in order to keep the issue open.
Thank you for all your contributions.

@eadz We generally don't accept feature requests here, and prefer [discuss](https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/) for that. However, I can see you may have an idea for a relatively small change with meaningful impact. How do you feel about writing a PR for this?

@eadz I get what you mean, sorry if it sounded like I was trying to push you out, I wasn't. What I meant was this is the current behavior, and changing it would either require significant work or introduce another way to generate this file (possibly) -- given that I would consider this a feature. But I can see how it's both a bug too given that UUIDs should Just Work™️ .

That said, I'm happy to take a look at providing a workaround for this, I was just reading into the internals of `bin/rails active_storage:install` so if you have any ideas or want to help contribute a patch let me know!
I will look into it. I think possibly the bug should be fixed in ActiveRecord as well.

@zzak 
Wdyt on something like this?
```diff
--- a/activestorage/db/migrate/20170806125915_create_active_storage_tables.rb
+++ b/activestorage/db/migrate/20170806125915_create_active_storage_tables.rb
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 class CreateActiveStorageTables < ActiveRecord::Migration[5.2]
   def change
-    create_table :active_storage_blobs do |t|
+    create_table :active_storage_blobs, id: primary_key_type do |t|
       t.string   :key,          null: false
       t.string   :filename,     null: false
       t.string   :content_type
@@ -18,10 +18,10 @@ def change
       t.index [ :key ], unique: true
     end

-    create_table :active_storage_attachments do |t|
+    create_table :active_storage_attachments, id: primary_key_type do |t|
       t.string     :name,     null: false
-      t.references :record,   null: false, polymorphic: true, index: false
-      t.references :blob,     null: false
+      t.references :record,   null: false, polymorphic: true, index: false, type: primary_key_type
+      t.references :blob,     null: false, type: primary_key_type

       if connection.supports_datetime_with_precision?
         t.datetime :created_at, precision: 6, null: false
@@ -30,15 +30,22 @@ def change
       end

       t.index [ :record_type, :record_id, :name, :blob_id ], name: "index_active_storage_attachments_uniqueness", unique: true
-      t.foreign_key :active_storage_blobs, column: :blob_id
+      t.foreign_key :active_storage_blobs, column: :blob_id, type: primary_key_type
     end

-    create_table :active_storage_variant_records do |t|
-      t.belongs_to :blob, null: false, index: false
+    create_table :active_storage_variant_records, id: primary_key_type do |t|
+      t.belongs_to :blob, null: false, index: false, type: primary_key_type
       t.string :variation_digest, null: false

       t.index %i[ blob_id variation_digest ], name: "index_active_storage_variant_records_uniqueness", unique: true
-      t.foreign_key :active_storage_blobs, column: :blob_id
+      t.foreign_key :active_storage_blobs, column: :blob_id, type: primary_key_type
     end
   end
+
+  private
+
+  def primary_key_type
+    config = Rails.application.config.generators
+    config.options[config.orm][:primary_key_type] || :bigint
+  end
 end
```

This is the simplest implementation I can think of. It checks which type is configured and uses it, or fallbacks to default.
@fatkodima It would help to see some tests, but I think this is a good step in the right direction 👍

review_comments: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/activerecord/lib/active_record/connection_adapters/abstract/schema_statements.rb#L296 -> the default argument is `:primary_key`, I think that's what should be provided here as a fallback. Currently your fallback value would be `:bigint`.
